Sending a request again after it failed or timed out.
A small request a load balancer or scheduler sends to see whether an instance can serve traffic.
Queries per second: how many requests arrive in each second.

before.note: The three prerequisite topics come first because the posts use their ideas freely. The four terms above are all the vocabulary the stages below assume.

stages.name: Basics
body: A server can finish only so much work each second. When more requests arrive than it can finish, it is overloaded. A cascading failure is a failure that grows over time through positive feedback: part of a system fails, which makes other parts more likely to fail [[sre-cascading]]. The SRE book's example is a service with several replicas. One replica fails from overload, the others take on its share and become more likely to fail, and the effect can take down every replica [[sre-cascading]].

The same chapter says overload is the most common cause of cascading failures [[sre-cascading]]. Amazon's engineers separate two numbers. Throughput is the total requests per second sent to a server. Goodput is the part of that traffic handled without errors and with low enough latency for the client to use the reply [[aws-load-shedding]].

The gap between them is the heart of the topic. When a server is so overloaded that its latency exceeds its client's timeout, requests start to fail [[aws-load-shedding]]. The server still does work for those requests, but nobody can use the result.

terms.definition: A failure that grows through positive feedback, as one failing part raises the odds that others fail.
The total number of requests per second sent to a server.
The part of throughput handled without errors and fast enough for the client to use the reply.
A loop in which a change causes more of the same change.

stages.name: How it works
body: The SRE book gives a simple case. A frontend in cluster A handles 1,000 requests per second. If cluster B fails, 1,200 requests per second arrive at A, which cannot handle them, so its frontends run out of resources, crash or miss deadlines, and the rate of successful requests falls well below 1,000 [[sre-cascading]]. That can spread: overloaded servers crash, the load balancing controller sends their requests to other clusters, and the overload becomes service-wide, possibly within a couple of minutes [[sre-cascading]].

Amazon explains why a server gets worse before it simply stops. In load tests, latency at low utilization is lower than at high utilization, because thread contention, context switching, garbage collection and I/O contention grow. At some point performance degrades much faster [[aws-load-shedding]]. Once the median response time reaches the client timeout, half of the requests time out, so availability is 50 percent. That is where a latency problem becomes an availability problem [[aws-load-shedding]].

Running out of one resource often leads to running out of another. The SRE chapter walks through CPU, memory, threads and file descriptors, and gives a chain in which poorly tuned garbage collection uses CPU, requests slow, memory fills, the cache shrinks, more requests reach the backend, and health checks start to fail. It warns that the symptoms can look like the root cause, which makes debugging hard [[sre-cascading]].

stages.name: Going deeper
body: Retries are the main amplifier. When a client times out, the server's progress on that request is wasted, and clients often retry, which multiplies the load. In a deep call graph where each layer retries, an overload at the bottom causes cascading retries that grow the load exponentially [[aws-load-shedding]]. The SRE chapter gives numbers: a backend that can take 10,000 requests per second per task, and a frontend that sends 10,100. The 100 that fail are retried, so the backend now sees 10,200, then more as retries grow. And if the backend, frontend and JavaScript layers each retry 3 times (4 attempts), one user action can cause 64 attempts at the database [[sre-cascading]].

The book's defences are plain. Retry with randomized exponential backoff. Limit retries per request, and consider a server-wide retry budget, for example 60 retries per minute in a process, after which requests simply fail. Decide whether a given layer should retry at all, and return a clear status when overloaded so that callers back off instead of retrying [[sre-cascading]].

Deadlines stop servers from working on requests nobody is waiting for. If a client set 10 seconds and the request reaches a thread after 11, the server should skip it [[sre-cascading]]. With deadline propagation, one deadline is set high in the stack and each hop gets what is left: a 30-second deadline with 7 seconds spent leaves 23 seconds for the next call [[sre-cascading]]. Amazon describes the same idea as a timeout hint sent with each request, which lets a server drop doomed requests at little cost [[aws-load-shedding]].

Queues and caches matter too. A queue ten times the thread count, with 100 ms of work per request, means a request that finds the queue full waits about 1.1 seconds, mostly in line, so for steady traffic the SRE book prefers short queues that reject early [[sre-cascading]]. A cache the service needs to carry its normal load (a capacity cache as opposed to a latency cache) makes every cold start risky, because an empty cache sends all requests to the slow path [[sre-cascading]].

stages.name: In practice and trade-offs
body: Load shedding is the main tool. When a server nears overload it rejects the excess so it can focus on requests it admits, which keeps their latency low and its goodput up. It is not free, and past a point goodput drops anyway [[aws-load-shedding]]. The SRE chapter lists where to shed: at reverse proxies, load balancers and individual tasks. It also warns that rate limiting often ignores overall service health, so it may not stop a failure that has begun, and simple versions leave capacity unused [[sre-cascading]]. The topic on rate limiting covers that mechanism.

Both sources insist on testing past the breaking point. Amazon wants goodput to plateau near full utilization and stay flat as load rises [[aws-load-shedding]]. The SRE chapter says to load test until failure and beyond, and to find out how far load must drop for a system to stabilize [[sre-cascading]]. Its example: a service healthy at 10,000 requests per second that starts crashing at 11,000 will almost certainly not stop crashing at 9,000, because only a small fraction of servers are healthy enough to take requests. The load has to fall much further [[sre-cascading]].

Recovery has its own steps in the book: add capacity if you have idle resources, stop health checks from killing tasks that are only starting up, restart wedged servers carefully, drop traffic (in a full crash loop, let through as little as 1 percent and ramp up slowly), serve degraded results, and pause batch work. Dropping traffic only helps if the cause is fixed, or the failure returns when load does [[sre-cascading]].

Shedding has trade-offs. If shedding and CPU-based scaling use a similar CPU target, scaling may never get the signal to add instances. A fleet that sheds may also run closer to its limit than CPU shows, which matters for losing an Availability Zone. And requests that fail fast can make median latency look good, so Amazon keeps them out of the latency metrics [[aws-load-shedding]]. The SRE book adds that a degraded mode used rarely is a code path likely to be broken, so it should be exercised regularly [[sre-cascading]].

terms.definition: Rejecting some requests as a server nears overload so it can finish the rest in time.
Doing less work per request, for example returning lower-quality results, to stay within capacity.
Servers that restart, are hit with a flood of traffic and fail again almost at once.
In the SRE book, a cache that lowers response time while the service can still carry its normal load with the cache empty.

misconceptions.myth: Adding more servers always fixes an overload.
misconceptions.truth: The SRE book says adding tasks can be the fastest fix when idle resources exist, but if the service is in a death spiral, more resources may not be enough [[sre-cascading]].

misconceptions.myth: More retries make a request more likely to succeed, so they are always safe.
misconceptions.truth: Each retry adds load to a service that may already be overloaded, and retries at several layers multiply, which can turn a small overload into a large one [[sre-cascading]] [[aws-load-shedding]].

misconceptions.myth: A server running flat out is doing useful work.
misconceptions.truth: Past its limit a server spends effort on replies that arrive after the client gave up, so throughput stays high while goodput falls [[aws-load-shedding]].

tryIt.intro: These two sources have no commands to run for this topic. The only code in them is a Go retry loop that the SRE chapter uses as an example of what to avoid, so it is not copied here. To practise, redo the arithmetic in Going deeper by hand: three layers with 4 attempts each is 4 x 4 x 4 attempts, and a retry budget of 60 per minute caps the extra requests a process can send.
